source_review.notes: Checked current official Apache Spark, Apache Flink, Apache Beam, Google Cloud Dataflow, Apache Iceberg, and Apache Kafka documentation plus the publisher record for the original Count-Min Sketch paper. All thirteen final references returned HTTP 200. Runtime-specific controls and thresholds are attributed rather than presented as universal behavior.

evidence: Reviewed per-key frequency, cost, fixed setup work, indivisible work, partition load, total work, mean load, and normalized maximum-load notation.
Checked the lower bound max(mean load, largest indivisible key work) and distinguished observed partition load from key-frequency proxies.
Checked salt fan-out, partial hot-key load, percentile, coefficient-of-variation, amplification, and service-level notation for consistent units and scopes.
notation_and_syntax.notes: Record count, bytes, CPU time, state, shuffle traffic, and elapsed time are treated as distinct load measures rather than interchangeable definitions of skew.

evidence: Executed the Python 3 fixture and reproduced 10,000,000 records, 200 partitions, an ideal mean of 50,000 records, and a 3,500,000-record hot key.
Recomputed the unsalted indivisible ratio as 3,500,000 divided by 50,000 = 70.0 and the hot-key share as 35.0 percent.
Recomputed the ideal 16-way salted hot-key partial as 218,750 records and its residual ratio to the original mean as 4.375.
numerical_recomputation.notes: The fixture demonstrates a lower bound and idealized salting effect; hash collisions, remainder distribution, non-hot work, fixed costs, and runtime overhead can increase realized load.

evidence: Verified total work is the sum of key work, mean partition load is total work divided by partition count, and maximum partition load cannot be below that mean.
Verified any indivisible key assigned wholly to one partition makes maximum partition load at least that key's work, yielding the stated combined lower bound.
Verified ideal fan-out divides the hot key's splittable contribution by the salt count while leaving nonsplittable setup, merge, and collision costs outside that ideal term.
symbolic_recomputation.notes: The bounds are necessary conditions, not predictions of scheduler, network, spill, garbage collection, cache, or downstream-service behavior.

evidence: Reviewed empty inputs, one key, one partition, more partitions than records, dominant null/default keys, monotonic keys, and composite-key collapse.
Reviewed skew in rows, bytes, CPU, state, fan-out, temporal windows, source partitions, sinks, storage files, and shared external resources.
Reviewed late data, retractions, retries, speculation, hot-key movement, changing distributions, bounded-state cleanup, and recovery bursts.
boundary_and_adversarial_cases.notes: Key skew, partition skew, temporal skew, resource skew, and amplification are diagnosed separately because each admits different mitigations and failure modes.

evidence: Traced salting through deterministic key expansion, local partial aggregation, unsalting, and final merge while preserving group membership and aggregate algebra requirements.
Checked skewed-join splitting against join type, duplicated-side uniqueness, null semantics, ordering, multiplicity, outer-row emission, and one-winner output publication.
Checked streaming repartitioning against keyed-state ownership, checkpoints, timers, watermarks, late-data policy, retractions, and bounded cleanup.
invariant_checking.notes: Mitigation is accepted only when output equivalence, state continuity, retry safety, and downstream contracts survive the changed partitioning plan.

evidence: Reviewed the mean-load and indivisible-key lower-bound argument and the consequence that adding partitions alone cannot split an unsplittable hot key.
Reviewed the two-level aggregation argument under associative and commutative merge operations and the counterexamples for order-sensitive or nonmergeable computations.
Reviewed skewed-join correctness conditions for replicating the bounded side and partitioning the hot side without duplicating or dropping logical matches.
proof_review.notes: Adaptive execution can improve a plan after observing statistics, but it does not prove balanced end-to-end work or semantic safety for arbitrary rewrites.

evidence: Audited heavy hitter, hot key, skewed partition, straggler, split, salt, fan-out, combine, replication, rebalance, adaptive execution, and amplification terminology.
Confirmed approximate sketch estimates are separated from exact verification and that one-sided Count-Min collision error is stated under the relevant assumptions.
Confirmed ideal lower bounds and idealized fan-out calculations are not labeled as measured runtime guarantees.
proof_sketch_labeling.notes: Algorithmic claims identify their assumptions; runtime mechanisms are examples of the general diagnosis-and-control model.

evidence: Reviewed per-key and per-partition records, bytes, CPU, elapsed time, spill, shuffle, state, backpressure, retries, errors, and resource saturation evidence.
Reviewed maximum-to-mean, percentiles, coefficient of variation, tail-task gaps, stage critical path, salt distribution, and pre/post mitigation amplification.
Confirmed measurements are segmented by execution, stage/operator, partition/key cohort, worker/resource, window, join side, file/source partition, and time.
empirical_evidence_labeling.notes: A frequency histogram, task-duration maximum, or runtime skew flag alone is not mislabeled as sufficient causal evidence.

conceptual_review.notes: Reviewed skew definitions, lower bounds, measurement units, exact/sample/sketch detection, key-versus-partition diagnosis, salting, two-level aggregation, join splitting, streaming state, temporal/resource skew, adaptive execution, amplification, experiments, and observability.

practitioner_review.notes: Reviewed implementable heavy-hitter verification, targeted fan-out, deterministic salting, bounded-side replication, semantic canaries, per-stage evidence, rollback conditions, capacity controls, and post-mitigation cost checks. Internal practitioner-oriented review only.

pedagogical_review.notes: Verified progression from load vocabulary and lower bounds through detection, diagnosis, safe mitigations, runtime adaptation, and operational proof. Ten examples and five answered exercises cover ratios, salting, metric disagreement, sketches, joins, state, temporal skew, amplification, experiments, and incident diagnosis.

limitations: Internal evidence record only; no external Spark/Flink/Beam/Dataflow/Iceberg/Kafka maintainer, distributed-data/runtime/storage/network/platform/SRE/security/economics specialist, production operator, paper author, downstream consumer, affected user, governance or accessibility specialist, or certification review is claimed.
